planting.note: Divide and transplant nursery-propagated rhizome clumps in fall into gritty, humus-rich, near-neutral soil that stays evenly moist but never waterlogged; purchase only propagated stock, since this federally threatened Great Lakes endemic must never be dug from the wild.

directions: Divide and transplant nursery-propagated rhizome clumps in fall into gritty, humus-rich, near-neutral soil that stays evenly moist but never waterlogged, mimicking the thin soils over limestone gravel along Great Lakes shorelines where this species is endemic. This diminutive iris spreads slowly into a dense groundcover and produces pale blue-violet flowers in mid-spring that are an early nectar source for queen bumblebees and other emerging native bees. Because it is federally listed as threatened, purchase only from nurseries selling propagated stock and never dig from wild populations. It makes an excellent choice for a shaded to partly sunny rock garden or shoreline restoration planting in the upper Midwest and Great Lakes basin.

planting.note: Sow seed directly into loose, well-drained sand in fall so it experiences natural winter cold-moist stratification; plant only nursery-grown seed-sourced stock, since this dune specialist is federally threatened.

directions: Sow seed directly into loose, well-drained sand in fall so it experiences natural winter cold-moist stratification, mimicking its native habitat on open, active Great Lakes sand dunes. This silvery, deeply lobed thistle spends several years as a low rosette before sending up a single flowering stalk of pale pink to cream blooms that are an important nectar source for native bees and migrating monarch butterflies, after which the plant sets seed and dies. It is a federally threatened dune specialist, so plant only nursery-grown seed-sourced stock and give it full sun and undisturbed, sandy, low-nutrient soil with excellent drainage. Established plantings help stabilize dune habitat while supporting pollinators that few other dune plants can sustain.

planting.note: Sow seed onto the surface of consistently saturated, acidic peat or sphagnum in fall so winter cold provides natural stratification, or transplant divided tussocks directly into a bog garden or constructed wetland.

directions: Sow seed onto the surface of consistently saturated, acidic peat or sphagnum in fall so winter cold provides natural stratification, or transplant divided tussocks directly into a bog garden or constructed wetland. Over years each plant builds a raised hummock of tightly packed leaf bases topped with fluffy white cottony seed heads in late spring, which provide nesting material for birds and cover for small wetland fauna. It is a keystone structural species of northern peatlands and bogs found across the Great Lakes region, and its tussocks help stabilize saturated, nutrient-poor soils where few other plants thrive. Best suited to a dedicated bog or rain-garden feature with permanently wet, acidic conditions rather than a typical border.

planting.note: Direct sow into saturated, acidic, peaty or muck soil in fall, allowing winter moisture and cold to break seed dormancy naturally.

directions: Direct sow into saturated, acidic, peaty or muck soil in fall, allowing winter moisture and cold to break seed dormancy naturally. Unlike the earlier-blooming, hummock-forming tussock cottongrass, this species spreads by rhizomes to form loose colonies and produces its tawny-brown cottony seed heads in late summer into fall, extending the bloom season in a bog or wet-meadow planting. The fluffy seed heads provide nesting fiber for birds and songbirds forage the seeds, while the dense root mass helps filter and stabilize saturated soils along pond and bog margins throughout the Appalachian and Great Lakes wetland range. Pair it with sundews, pitcher plants, or sedges for an authentic acidic bog planting.

planting.note: Establish rooted cuttings or small nursery transplants in spring into loose, infertile, well-drained sand; seed germination is notoriously slow and uneven, so cuttings are the more reliable method.

directions: Establish rooted cuttings or small nursery transplants in spring into loose, infertile, well-drained sand, since this wiry, gray-green, heather-like shrublet is adapted to the driest, most exposed dune and sandplain sites around the Great Lakes and Atlantic coast. Its tiny bright-yellow flowers open only in full sun for a few hours at a time in late spring but are visited by small native bees and flies, and its dense mat of scale-like foliage provides cover for ground-nesting insects and helps anchor loose sand against wind erosion. It requires excellent drainage and low fertility to thrive and quickly rots in heavy, moisture-retentive soils. An excellent, tough groundcover choice for a sandy, sun-baked native dune or gravel garden.
